nodes.label: HARK Installer Stick
nodes.desc: How a box gets built. One USB stick, no internet needed, no keypresses: it installs Debian, encrypts the disk, seals the key to the machine's TPM chip so it unlocks itself, then installs HARK on first boot.
nodes.tech: build-usb-offline.sh → hark-installer-offline.iso (4.0 GB) · Debian DVD-1 + 81 clevis/tpm2 debs + 741 appliance debs (Node 22, Chromium, cage, Postgres, NetworkManager, Tailscale, AMD graphics firmware) · flash-usb.sh self-verifies the stick and refuses to write otherwise
nodes.notes:
The bar it had to clear: plug it in, it comes up, nobody types anything, ever. A monitoring box that doesn't come back after a power cut is a guaranteed outage.

⛔ The plan of using systemd-cryptenroll for the TPM does NOT work on Debian at all — the boot image contains zero TPM code, so the box would ask a grower for a passphrase forever. clevis is the fix, and it installs its own unlock path into the boot image.
⛔ Do NOT delete the passphrase keyslot after sealing. hark123 is the recovery path; without it a dead motherboard is an unrecoverable disk.
⚠️ Pull the stick the moment an install finishes on a box that boots USB first, or the next power-on silently re-wipes the install you just did.
⛔ NEVER flash hark-installer-debug.iso — its console goes to a serial port the Beelink doesn't have, so the screen stays blank.

Traps found building it, each of which would have stranded Max at the hardware: Debian's ISO sets no menu timeout, so with no keyboard it waits forever; unattended flags must go BEFORE the --- on the kernel line; /sys/block/*/removable is 0 for USB flash drives, so a removable-check picks the boot stick itself and dies 'disk too small'; a cdrom apt source blocks forever on 'please insert the disc'; and never put real work in late_command — it goes through several shells and mangles quotes. ☠️ The packaging trap cost two full build cycles: --download-only in a container only fetches what that container is MISSING, so 265 debs staged and zero installed, with a clean dpkg -C because nothing was half-installed. Never treat a clean dpkg -C as proof software is present — check the binaries.
